papers.title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy–Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
papers.tldr: Kumo Tabular is an open family of TabPFN-style tabular foundation models (27M to 214M parameters) pretrained only on synthetic tables; the largest ranks first on eight benchmarks including TabArena and TALENT, and predicts 36 times faster than LimiX-2 on TabArena.
summary: Tabular foundation models that predict new tables in-context, with no training, are now competitive with tuned tree ensembles, but the strongest ones tend to be slow and hard to scale to very large tables. There is room for models that are both more accurate and sit on the accuracy-speed frontier, with open weights.

The NVIDIA team trains three sizes (S 27M, M 61M, L 214M parameters) purely on artificial tables drawn from their "Kumo prior". A table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts unlabeled rows from labeled ones; architectural changes target training stability and let the model scale to about 150M cells on modern GPUs. They evaluate on eight benchmarks covering classification, probabilistic regression, very large tables (over 1M rows or 100K columns) and tables with strings, text or images.

Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on all eight benchmarks (TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, TabBench-Bio), and accuracy grows with model size in every tested comparison. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena, and the L model is 36 times faster than LimiX-2 on TabArena and 1.7 times faster than TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena. Takeaway: this is a new strong, open-weights baseline (weights under OpenMDW-1.1, pretraining code under Apache 2.0) that any tabular FM or tabular SSL comparison should now include, and the row-embedding plus ICL design is reusable. Caveat: it is an industry preprint whose benchmark wins are self-reported; independent leaderboard replication is still needed.

papers.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
papers.source: arXiv cs.CL, accepted at the UniReps Workshop (NeurIPS 2026)
papers.tldr: Along a family of directions from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the plain mean difference, the best probe is not the best steering vector: steering favors directions near the mean difference in 59 of 60 layer-model-concept settings, and probes transfer across models better than steering vectors do.
summary: Probe directions are routinely reused as steering vectors, assuming that the direction that best detects a concept also best changes it. Whether detection and control actually prefer the same direction, and whether they transfer across models the same way, has not been tested carefully.

Using three instruction-tuned models from different families, the authors build a one-parameter family of directions that interpolates between a covariance-adjusted linear discriminant and the class mean difference. They compare probing accuracy and additive steering effect along this family at a fixed side-effect budget for truthfulness and sentiment, with a layer sweep, matched probe and steering texts, and a rotation-based steering operator as a check. Cross-model transfer uses a linear map fitted on neutral text.

In every model the best probe differs from the best steering direction, and steering favors directions closer to the mean difference in 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations. For sentiment an intermediate direction can steer 27-56% more strongly, but that gain shrinks with matched texts and depends on layer and operator. Transferred probes keep 81-91% of above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference loses more of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs (only three pairs pass their predefined criteria). On PopQA, steering toward "unknown" raises abstention by 18-44 points on uncertain errors versus 2-5 on confident ones. Takeaway for steering-geometry work: do not assume a discriminative (whitened) probe is a good control direction; the mean difference is the safer default, and probe and steering geometry should be reported separately. Limitations: three models and two main concepts, workshop paper.

papers.title: Pretty Linear Liars: Unregularized Probes Favor Intervention-Unfaithful Features
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability as a Science (InterpScience)
papers.tldr: Unregularized least-squares probes amplify low-variance, spuriously correlated directions, so their features are not what the model uses; a moderate ridge penalty maximizes intervention faithfulness and yields directions close to those found by optimizing interventions directly.
summary: Linear probes are a staple of mechanistic interpretability, yet a decodable feature is not necessarily one the network uses. Intervention faithfulness is the better criterion, but how probe regularization affects whether the discovered direction is causal had not been studied systematically.

The authors analyze ordinary least squares probes and ridge probes of increasing strength, first theoretically and then empirically in a toy transformer and in Llama-2-7B. They measure intervention faithfulness, i.e. whether pushing activations along the probe direction changes the output as the ground truth predicts, and compare against directions learned by directly optimizing intervention outcomes.

Theory shows OLS probes amplify low-variance activation directions that correlate spuriously with the target, while regularization suppresses them. Empirically, faithfulness rises with regularization up to a point and then falls, and the best-regularized probes closely match intervention-optimized directions in both direction and variance; the abstract gives no headline numbers. Takeaway: when a probe direction is used to steer, edit or explain (for example concept or prototype directions), tune the ridge strength for intervention faithfulness rather than for probe loss, and treat the lowest-loss probe with suspicion. Limitations: one toy model and one 7B LLM, workshop paper.

papers.title: Representational Change Under Self-Consuming Training: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis
papers.tldr: Across five generations of training on model-generated text, SAEs trained on the original model degrade progressively, and fine-tuning restores reconstruction but not feature usefulness: task information spreads out instead of staying in a few latents.
summary: Future LLMs will increasingly be trained on their predecessors' outputs, but work on these self-consuming loops has focused on output quality, not on what happens to internal representations. It is also unclear whether SAEs, a main tool for reading those representations, stay reliable when the model drifts.

The authors train a lineage over five self-consuming generations on synthetic data alongside a matched control trained on real data with identical settings. They test zero-shot transfer of SAEs trained before self-consumption, measuring reconstruction and sparsity across SAE widths, architectures and layers, then fine-tune the original SAE on each generation and use sparse probing to check whether task-relevant information stays concentrated in a few latents.

Zero-shot SAE performance degrades steadily with self-consumption, with reconstruction and sparsity gaps that vary strongly by layer. Fine-tuning largely recovers reconstruction, but task-relevant information becomes less concentrated in individual features, though it is still present in the full latent space. Takeaway: good reconstruction after adapting an SAE to a shifted model (fine-tuned, domain-adapted or retrained) does not show the features are still interpretable; check sparse-probing or feature-level metrics too. Caveat: the abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes, and results come from small Pythia-scale models.

papers.title: Get Hint-Augmented GRPO Done Right Through Activation Steering
papers.tldr: ASH trains a steering vector during GRPO to capture the behavioral shift a hint induces, then injects it at inference without any hint, fixing the train-test mismatch of hint-augmented GRPO and raising average pass@8 of Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Base by 2.60% and 2.21%.
summary: GRPO gets no gradient when every sampled answer to a hard question fails. Hint-augmented GRPO adds hints to make such questions solvable, but no hint exists at test time, so the training and inference contexts mismatch and gains are inconsistent.

The authors reframe a hint as a steering signal and propose ASH (Activation Steering for Hinting). During training the model sees both hinted and plain questions, and a trainable steering vector is optimized to widen the margin between generation probabilities under the hinted versus plain context, capturing the question-agnostic part of the hint's effect. At inference this vector is added to the activations with no hint in the prompt. They test on Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Base and Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct.

ASH consistently improves pass@k on AMC, OlympiadBench, AIME24 and AIME25 and on out-of-distribution Minerva and GPQA-Diamond, with average pass@8 gains of 2.60% (Qwen3-1.7B-Base) and 2.21% (Qwen3-4B-Base). Takeaway: a learned, question-agnostic steering vector can distill a context-dependent behavior (here a hint) into the activations, a pattern that could transfer to other prompt-only behaviors. Caveats: only models up to 4B parameters, and gains are a few points.

papers.title: The Geometry of Conceptors in Neural-Activation Spaces
papers.tldr: Conceptors (soft subspace filters) decompose exactly into a pole average, a mean-separation update and a covariance-shape update; across five LMs the extra directions beyond the mean-difference line help, bipolar fitting amplifies both poles more reliably, and conceptor steering beats three mean-based controls in generation win rate.
summary: Most concept directions and steering vectors are single mean-difference vectors, while conceptors represent a concept as a graded set of directions. How a conceptor's geometry depends on the contrast used to fit it (opposing poles versus presence and absence) has not been worked out.

The authors derive an exact decomposition of a centered pooled conceptor into an average pole filter, a mean-separation update and a covariance-shape update, and compare bipolar with unipolar fitting. They run experiments on five language models for sentiment, political leaning and stance, and depression expression, covering held-out contrast reconstruction, amplification, layerwise probing, subspace removal and a generation evaluation.

Both the mean-separation and covariance-shape updates improve reconstruction of held-out contrasts, so directions beyond the mean-difference line carry real variation, and the comparator changes how much they help. Bipolar fits raise evidence for both poles more consistently than unipolar fits, conceptor size (quota) correlates positively with layerwise probe performance, and cross-concept overlap predicts interference under subspace removal. In generation, conceptor filters win more often against an unsteered reference than three mean-based controls. Takeaway for steering geometry: the choice of contrast is a geometric decision, and a subspace (conceptor) view gives measurable handles (size, overlap) for interference between concepts. Caveat: the abstract reports no effect sizes.

papers.title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
papers.tldr: With 227 validated minimal pairs on 14 open models, the attention heads that flip moral answers turn out to form a general normative-evaluation circuit (same effect share for moral and non-moral norms), and the located SAE features mostly respond to the cue word "morally" rather than moral content.
summary: Interpretability studies find attention heads and SAE features that change a model's answer to moral prompts, but these components could reflect moral content, any normative judgment, or just the word "morally". Without controls, "moral circuits" and "moral features" may be mislabeled.

The authors build 227 minimal phrase pairs, validated by five annotators, that differ in a moral standard, a different norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics, evidence) or a descriptive quality. They test 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned) with and without the word "morally", using head ablations, trained SAE dictionaries and linear directions, plus 400 ETHICS scenarios.

The heads that change the moral answer carry the same share of the effect for moral and other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% CI [0.92, 1.07] with the word; 0.90 [0.84, 0.96] without), and removing them erases 37-39% of the acceptable-versus-unacceptable gap on ETHICS versus 1-3% for ten random heads. The located SAE features respond mostly to the word "morally". The annotated category is linearly readable, and removing its direction weakens moral verdicts by a few percent in the eight models tested. Takeaway: before naming a circuit or SAE feature after a concept, test it against matched control concepts and cue-word ablations; otherwise lexical cues masquerade as semantics. Pairs, ratings, code, SAE dictionaries and results are released.

papers.title: Interpretable deep concepts of organoid morphology
papers.tldr: SAEs trained on DINOv3 and the organoid-specific ViTAMIn-O turn black-box organoid image features into spatially labeled concepts; filtering concepts by spatial label improves downstream AUROC on three of five tasks and exposed a preprocessing confounder in one task.
summary: Foundation-model features beat handcrafted ones for classifying organoid morphology (drug response, viability, differentiation), but their black-box nature hides which morphological cues a classifier uses. This is the same trust problem faced by any biomedical imaging model built on frozen foundation features.

The authors train sparse autoencoders on representations from DINOv3 (general purpose) and ViTAMIn-O (organoid specific). Each learned concept is annotated with a spatial label (organoid, organoid wall, background), and they compute concept dataset-specificity and task relevance across five downstream tasks.

Spatial labels of DINOv3-SAE concepts produce coarse organoid segmentations on out-of-domain datasets, and keeping only concepts with suitable spatial labels improves downstream AUROC on three of the five tasks. Inspecting the most relevant concepts revealed a confounding factor caused by the authors' own preprocessing in one task. Takeaway for medical imaging: an SAE over frozen foundation features is a cheap way to audit what a classifier relies on and to catch shortcuts, and spatially filtering concepts can even help accuracy, an approach that could carry over to ultrasound encoders. Caveats: the abstract gives no AUROC values, and SAEs will be released only on publication.

papers.title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: VLMs fail at cross-image matching even though the answer is decodable from their hidden states; the comparison runs through 16-32 attention heads, and training only those heads' query/key projections (0.02% of parameters) adds 28.3 points on SPair-71k for Qwen3-VL-8B.
summary: Vision-language models often fail to match a point or object across two images even when their own hidden states contain the answer. Knowing where this information is lost is needed to fix it efficiently.

The study traces the computation from visual tokens to the answer in Qwen3-VL (2B to 32B), InternVL3.5-8B and Gemma-3-12B on synthetic shape matching, HPatches point correspondence and SPair-71k semantic correspondence. It uses answer-position probes, probe-direction steering, mass-preserving redistribution of cross-image attention in selected heads, and head-restricted fine-tuning, with decision rules frozen before each run.

Probes beat the calibrated output by 15-25 points in every family, yet steering along the probe direction changes no more answers than random directions. Perturbing the attention of 16-32 heads removes 17-22 points on synthetic and 15-32 on HPatches, versus at most 7 for control heads; training only those heads' query and key projections adds 28.3 (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 (InternVL3.5-8B) points on SPair-71k and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the same heads. Takeaway: probe-decodable is not steerable, and circuit localization can pick a tiny, effective fine-tuning target. Caveat: single-author preprint, correspondence tasks only.

papers.title: Weights & Caches: LLMs Can Program Tabular Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Without gradient descent, an LLM (GPT-6 Astra) writes nanoTabPFN weights from scratch (mean ROC AUC 0.849 on 20 TabArena datasets vs 0.876 pretrained), repairs a regression failure in TabPFN-3.5, and writes KV-cache edits that steer its predictions.
summary: Neural networks are normally programmed by optimization, but recent work suggests LLMs can reason about and write network weights directly. Tabular foundation models are a natural test bed because their parameters implement inference across many datasets.

The Freiburg and Prior Labs authors use GPT-6 Astra in three settings with no gradient-based optimization: writing nanoTabPFN weights from zero initialization, diagnosing and repairing a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, and writing KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5 predictions on unseen synthetic datasets.

The LLM-programmed nanoTabPFN reaches a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets versus 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. The repair restores near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic data with only a 0.08% average relative error increase on TabArena-Lite, and cache edits can reverse linear trends or turn sine waves into approximate square waves without changing weights. Takeaway: KV-cache editing is a weight-free intervention handle on TabPFN-style models, useful both for interpretability and for targeted fixes. Caveats: depends on a frontier proprietary LLM, and steering is shown only on synthetic data.

papers.title: A Bag of Concepts? Testing Role-Filler Binding in the Verbalizable Workspace
papers.source: arXiv cs.CL, accepted at Interpretability as a Science Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
papers.tldr: Lens-based "verbalizable workspace" monitors carry directions that steer what a model says about roles but not the role-filler bindings it computes: probes read roles near ceiling from the residual stream yet below a random control from the workspace.
summary: Runtime alignment monitors that read a model's "verbalizable workspace" are proposed for catching silent cognition, but most safety-relevant propositions are relational ("the model plans to deceive the user" versus the reverse). A monitor is only useful if the workspace preserves who fills which role.

On Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-3-12B and Gemma-3-27B-IT, the authors test two lens families (J-lens and R-lens) and two ways of fitting a role direction (difference of means and LRE-gradient), using linear probes, steering along the role direction with strength-matched controls, and ablation of the top ten lens directions against rank-matched random subspaces.

Linear probes recover role near ceiling from the residual stream but score below a rank-matched random control when reading the workspace, and steering along the role direction changes binding no more than control edits. Ablating the workspace damages binding only in Gemma-3-27B-IT, where scale and instruction tuning are confounded. Takeaway: a direction that steers verbal output need not be the representation the model computes with, so monitors and steering claims need binding-specific controls. Limitations: three models and a workshop paper.

papers.title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
papers.tldr: Extending the refusal-direction recipe, difference-of-means "abstention directions" for query ambiguity, knowledge limits and safety each steer abstention up or down from middle layers, and they share a common component because steering one shifts the others.
summary: LLMs abstain for three distinct reasons: an ambiguous query, missing knowledge, or a conflict with human values. Prior representation work only studied the last case via the refusal direction, so it is unknown whether the three share internal structure.

For each reason the authors build counterfactual prompt pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute a normalized difference-of-means abstention direction. They then add or subtract these directions at different layers and measure abstention.

Intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention for all three perspectives, and steering with one direction also affects the others, pointing to a shared directional component. Takeaway: abstention and refusal look like one partly shared axis, so steering against refusal may also suppress honest "I don't know" answers; the template-matched counterfactual pairs are a clean recipe for extracting other directions. Caveat: the abstract gives no numbers, models or effect sizes, so the strength of the effects cannot be judged from it.
